After completing all the procedures and finalizing the surgery date with the doctor, we were informed that the surgery could not proceed because their cashless department denied my insurance. The staff member said they do not have a good experience with Tata AIG and therefore do not provide cashless service for this particular insurance holder. Instead, they demanded a 100% cash deposit for the surgery..........
I would not have had any issue if this had been clearly communicated during my first visit. During my initial appointment, I specifically asked whether you provide cashless services. The receptionist said yes and asked which insurance company I had. I clearly informed them that it was Tata AIG.....
Today, after completing all the required eye reports and finalizing everything, we were told at the last moment that we must pay the full amount in advance. If I have to pay 100% in cash, then what is the point of opting for a cashless service??????.......
If your clinic does not provide cashless services for Tata AIG insurance holders, then please remove it from your network list and inform patients clearly during the first visit.............
No hard feelings, but this situation caused unnecessary stress and wasted both my time and money.  & I didn’t want to post a negative comment, but I’m leaving this here to help anyone with Tata AIG insurance avoid the same situation.

If reimbursement was the only option, I should have been clearly informed earlier. Arranging a 100% advance payment at the last moment is difficult and defeats the purpose of opting for a cashless insurance policy....................
My request is simply that patients should be clearly informed in advance if cashless service is not available for a particular insurance provider, so they can plan accordingly and avoid unnecessary stress, time, and expense.

By Dr. Jignesh M. Gala — Vitreoretinal & Cataract Surgeon, Crystal Clear Eye Clinic, Andheri West, Mumbai

In June 2017, I travelled to Kuching, Malaysia, to sit one of the most practical and intensely hands-on examinations in clinical ophthalmology — the Refraction Certificate Examination of The Royal College of Ophthalmologists (RCOphth), London. There were no multiple-choice questions to revise for. There were no written papers to write. There was no oral viva on a textbook subject. For the duration of the examination, I moved from one clinical station to the next, with a different patient at each, an examiner watching every move, and a retinoscope or trial frame in my hand.

I passed on my first attempt. The official letter from the College, dated 14 July 2017, signed by Susannah Grant, Head of the Examinations Department, confirms the result. But the bigger point of this post is not the result. It is the examination itself — and what an exam structured this way is really testing.

The Refraction Certificate of The Royal College of Ophthalmologists is the examination that, in 2017, formally certified that I could be trusted to take those measurements correctly. The College gave me a piece of paper that summer. The skills behind that piece of paper, I bring to work every day.
